case_analysis.thread_summary: The thread concerns delays in starting Bluetooth RF PHY qualification testing because the provided customer test procedure did not adequately explain how to enter and control Bluetooth Low Energy Direct Test Mode (DTM) for automated RF PHY testing. The test lab identified that the existing documentation only covered RF regulatory test mode procedures and lacked instructions for connecting the InterLab qualification tester through UART/USB control paths. Qualcomm reference documentation was later provided to clarify the DTM control mechanism and associated tooling requirements. The discussion then shifted to practical troubleshooting of the Qualcomm DTM utility, required runtime dependencies, COM port configuration, and tester connection setup needed to execute RF PHY qualification tests.
case_analysis.key_technical_discussion: The main technical issue was the distinction between generic RF DUT test mode procedures and Bluetooth RF PHY qualification DTM procedures required for automated InterLab tester operation. The consultant identified that the original customer documentation lacked explicit instructions for UART/USB-controlled DTM operation and automated tester integration. Qualcomm documentation introduced the use of the QC.BluetoothLE_DirectMode.exe utility, including requirements to copy the executable into the QDART BIN directory and configure COM ports for tester communication. Additional troubleshooting revealed that the executable depended on associated DLL and possibly OCX files that also needed to be copied for successful launch. The thread also clarified that the external PC acts as a serial pass-through bridge between the InterLab tester and the DUT, with specific serial configuration requirements including HCI-Serial mode and 115.2 kbps COM settings.
case_analysis.key_decision_logic: The consultant's reasoning focused on verifying whether the supplied qualification procedure truly supported Bluetooth RF PHY qualification requirements rather than only regulatory RF testing. The key decision process was to validate that the DUT could enter Bluetooth LE DTM under tester control and communicate correctly with the InterLab system through supported serial interfaces. Once the Qualcomm reference material was obtained, the consultant used the vendor-specific implementation details to bridge the documentation gap and iteratively troubleshoot the runtime environment, dependencies, and communication configuration needed for automated RF PHY testing.
case_analysis.risk_if_done_wrong: If the issue were handled incorrectly, RF PHY qualification testing could not start despite reserved lab schedules, causing qualification delays and wasted test preparation effort. Misinterpreting RF regulatory test mode as equivalent to Bluetooth RF PHY DTM support could result in incomplete qualification capability verification and failed automated tester integration. Missing executable dependencies or incorrect COM port setup could lead to repeated failed DTM connection attempts and extended debugging time during scheduled qualification activities.
case_analysis.consulting_mistake: An initial assumption was made that copying only the QC.BluetoothLE_DirectMode.exe utility into the QDART directory would be sufficient to enable DTM operation. Testing later revealed that the executable depended on additional DLL and possibly OCX files located in the original directory. The issue was corrected by recognizing the dependency relationship and instructing that all associated runtime files be copied together before retrying execution.
case_analysis.consulting_takeaway: For Bluetooth RF PHY qualification, consultants must explicitly verify that the DUT supports Bluetooth LE DTM operation under automated tester control and that the documentation includes complete tester integration procedures, not just RF regulatory test modes. Vendor-specific DTM utilities often depend on additional runtime files and serial interface configuration details that are not obvious from high-level qualification instructions. Early validation of tester communication flow, COM port mapping, and software dependencies can prevent major qualification schedule delays.
